group: PSI Score: Pneumonia Severity Index for CAP
question:
Patient note:
A 63-year-old woman was brought to the emergency department by her sister after four days of progressive cough producing rust-colored sputum, intermittent chills, and pleuritic discomfort along the left posterior thorax that had become constant overnight; she described needing to sleep propped on two pillows because lying flat worsened her shortness of breath. She lives independently in a single-family home, prepares her own meals, and had been able to walk several blocks each evening despite chronic systolic dysfunction related to a remote anterior myocardial infarction, for which she takes carvedilol, sacubitril-valsartan, and low-dose furosemide. She also carries a diagnosis of compensated stage A cirrhosis secondary to nonalcoholic steatohepatitis, followed every six months in hepatology clinic, with the most recent ultrasound three months earlier showing no ascites or lesions and her last liver panel demonstrating mildly elevated transaminases but preserved synthetic function; she has never required paracentesis, encephalopathy therapy, or variceal banding. She denied prior strokes, transient neurologic deficits, chronic kidney problems, dialysis, malignancy, or recent hospitalizations, and reported the last time she received any antibiotic was for an uncomplicated urinary tract infection more than a year ago. Social history revealed lifelong abstinence from tobacco, only occasional wine with dinner, and no illicit drug use. She is up to date on her adult immunizations except for this season’s influenza booster, had no recent travel, and was unaware of sick contacts at work. Review of systems was negative for headache, visual changes, confusion, abdominal pain, dysuria, or rash. Upon arrival she was seated upright on the cart, conversant, and fully oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Initial vital signs obtained by triage were temperature 38.5 °C orally, heart rate 99 beats per minute and regular, respiratory rate 23 breaths per minute with shallow inspirations, blood pressure 112/68 mm Hg, and pulse oximetry 90 % on ambient air that improved to 94 % after placement of 2 L/min nasal cannula. Skin was warm and well perfused without jaundice or spider angiomata, sclerae anicteric, and oral mucosa moist. Jugular venous pulsation was not elevated when reclined to 30°. Cardiac examination disclosed a displaced point of maximal impulse and a soft third heart sound but no murmurs or pericardial rub. Lungs revealed coarse inspiratory crackles and egophony in the left lower posterior field with dullness to percussion; breath sounds were otherwise vesicular without wheezes, and there was no tactile fremitus over the right lung. Extremities were warm without edema or clubbing. Abdomen was soft and non-distended with a palpable but non-tender liver edge three centimeters below the costal margin, no shifting dullness, and active bowel sounds. Neurologic survey showed equal pupils, intact extraocular movements, fluent speech, symmetric strength, and normal heel-to-shin testing. An ECG demonstrated sinus rhythm at 98 beats per minute with known Q-wave pattern but no new ischemic changes. Portable posterior-anterior chest radiograph obtained before any medications were administered displayed a dense consolidation occupying the lingular and left lower lobe segments with air bronchograms; the costophrenic angles remained sharp, and there was no evidence of cardiomegaly beyond her baseline. Arterial blood gas on room air, drawn prior to supplemental oxygen, revealed pH 7.41, PaCO₂ 37 mm Hg, and PaO₂ 65 mm Hg. Initial laboratory studies showed white blood cell count 14 600/µL with 82 % neutrophils, hematocrit 37 %, platelets 190 000/µL, basic metabolic panel notable for sodium 135 mEq/L, potassium 4.0 mEq/L, chloride 100 mEq/L, bicarbonate 24 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 26 mg/dL, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, and serum glucose 125 mg/dL measured on a non-fasting sample. Aspartate and alanine aminotransferases were 62 U/L and 58 U/L respectively, total bilirubin 1.0 mg/dL, albumin 3.9 g/dL, and international normalized ratio 1.2. A lactate level was 1.8 mmol/L. Bedside ultrasound demonstrated a collapsible inferior vena cava and normal renal corticomedullary differentiation without hydronephrosis. Urinalysis was bland. No medications other than acetaminophen taken at home had been ingested during this illness, and she had received no intravenous fluids, antibiotics, diuretics, or oxygen therapy before the described measurements except for the brief nasal cannula placement used to obtain the post-room-air saturation. The emergency physician completed her assessment while the patient remained hemodynamically stable, awake, and interactive, reporting her primary concern as “just wanting to breathe easier and stop coughing.”

Question: What is the patient's Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI), using pretreatment findings:
- Demographics: for a woman, start with age minus 10: 63 − 10 = 53. She lives independently, so nursing-home residence adds 0.
- Comorbidities: cirrhosis counts as liver disease even when compensated (+20); chronic systolic heart failure adds 10. Malignancy, cerebrovascular disease, and renal disease are absent (+0 each).
- Examination: normal mentation, RR 23 (<30/min), systolic BP 112 (≥90 mmHg), temperature 38.5 °C (neither <35 nor ≥40), and pulse 99 (<125/min) → 0 each.
- Labs and oxygenation: pH 7.41 (≥7.35), BUN 26 (<30 mg/dL), sodium 135 (≥130 mEq/L), glucose 125 (<250 mg/dL), and hematocrit 37% (≥30%) → 0 each. Room-air PaO₂ 65 mmHg is not <60, and saturation 90% is not <90% → 0.
- Imaging: consolidation without pleural effusion → 0.
Sum: 53 + 20 + 10 = 83 (risk class III).
Final answer: 83
